title: Ephemeral reservation accounting audit and burst-charge reconciliation
creator: Maya Chen
description: Summary: During a capacity incident on 2025-02-09 we observed repeated eviction storms in a Dedicated cluster caused by a combination of ephemeral reservation over-allocation and an edge-case leak in KV cache accounting. Symptoms: sudden tenant throughput increase, reservation growth beyond configured quota, and burst_token_bucket draining without proper refunds. Root cause hypothesis: a codepath in the batch allocator created transient reservations (ephemeral_reservations) for short-lived requests but failed to decrement the reservation ledger when KV cache entries expired or when requests hit a retry path. This produced incorrect billing attribution and allowed a noisy tenant to consume more soft capacity than intended, triggering neighbor contention and cascading scale events.
steps_taken: 1) Immediate mitigation: applied a soft-fence on the affected tenant group and disabled ephemeral reservation creation for new short-lived task types. 2) Reconciled ledger for the incident window (2025-02-09 03:10–04:22 UTC) using telemetry snapshots to refund burst tokens and correct billing. 3) Rolled a temporary patch to enforce TTL-based decrement of ephemeral_reservations in the allocator. 4) Deployed enhanced metering to capture reservation lifecycle events and KV cache reference counts. 5) Notified impacted customers and opened billing remediation tickets where appropriate.
decision_log: - Short-term: keep soft-fence active for affected tenants until reconciliation and autoscaler policy review complete. - Medium-term: implement strict accounting for ephemeral_reservations with a bounded reconciler loop running asynchronously; add unit tests for retry/error paths that previously leaked. - Long-term: introduce a burst-accounting ledger and token refund window (30s) so that retries/evictions refund tokens deterministically. Trade-offs considered: synchronously decrementing reservations reduces leak surface but can add tail latency; we chose asynchronous reconciliation plus strong invariants and monitoring to avoid latency regressions.

acceptance_criteria: - Reconciler runs on canary cluster and closes 99% of ephemeral reservation leaks in a synthetic test within 60 seconds. - No latency regression (>5th percentile) in canary traffic after reconciler enabled. - Telemetry emissions for reservation lifecycle appear in Grafana panels and alert if discrepancy >1% between created and decremented counts.

mitigation_playbook: Short term: 1) Apply soft-fence to suspect tenant IDs, 2) Disable ephemeral reservation feature flag, 3) Kick off manual reconciler job for the incident window, 4) Notify billing and customer success for refunds. Recovery steps are documented in runbook_patch_v1.md. Long term: reconciler + ledger + stricter admission heuristics for ephemeral reservations.
retrospective_notes: Key lessons: (1) accounting invariants are fundamental to burst-safety — we must treat reservation lifecycle as first-class and instrument it at creation and destruction. (2) Async reconciliation allows us to keep tail latency stable while providing eventual correctness but requires strong alerting. (3) We lacked a clear billing reconciliation workflow; that is now codified in the playbook. Follow-ups: expand canary coverage and add a reconciliation SLT (service level target) for reservation drift.
